blurb: The pink one: the same silver-grey felted mat as its little sister, but with rose-tinted bracts that give the flower clusters a distinct blush. CSU lists the two together, and they are used interchangeably as a tough, walkable groundcover.
water: Low to moderate; occasional deep soak in summer heat
spread: Mat-forming: creeps outward by short stolons into a spreading silver-grey carpet
seasons: Rose-pink 'cat toe' clusters late spring into summer over a silver-grey mat that persists through winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 11,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun to part shade, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Well-drained soil, as for the whole genus. Gritty, lean ground; it will rot at the crown in a wet, heavy spot.[1]
care.water: Low to moderate. CSU rates its moisture requirement low to moderate, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of spreading. A spreading mat of silver-grey foliage with clustered flowerheads like cat toes — CSU lists it alongside littleleaf pussytoes for flagstones and rock gardens.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers from spring into midsummer; CSU records the colour as pink, white and the height as 2–6 in tall.[1]
care.maintenance: Low. Cut old growth back in late winter or early spring rather than in fall, so the stems hold snow and give the crown some cover. Skip fertilizer: lean soil keeps these natives compact and long-lived.[1][2]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

references.name: CSU Extension — Native Herbaceous Perennials for Colorado Landscapes (fact sheet 7.242, PDF: complete Table 1)
CSU Extension — Xeriscaping: Perennials and Annual Flowers (7.231)

edible.summary: No documented culinary use; a native mat groundcover and butterfly host plant.[1]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for rosy pussytoes, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it, and don't reason across from any other plant in this guide. Like its relatives it is a larval host for painted lady and American lady butterflies, which is a much better reason to grow it.[1]
